title: Advanced Basics
lead: Work in bulk, not one by one: find files with `find`, process them with `xargs`, redirect streams, build pipelines and write your first small script.
objectives: Find files with `find` by name, type, size, time and permissions
Know the difference between `-exec ... {} \;`, `-exec ... {} +` and `xargs`; list first before `-delete`
Summarise logs with pipelines such as `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`
Recognise the pitfalls of quoting (`'...'` and `"..."`), globs and brace expansion
Use exit codes, `&&`/`||`, shebang, `chmod +x` and `./script.sh` to run small scripts

sections.title: find: searching in depth
body: `find <start> <conditions> <action>` walks the directory tree and processes every path that meets the conditions. With no conditions it lists everything. With no action the default is `-print`.
Key rule: **quote your patterns**. If you type `find . -name *.log`, the shell expands `*.log` against files in the current directory before `find` even starts, and the result will surprise you.
List first, act later: before a dangerous action (`-delete`, `-exec rm`) run the same command without the action and read the output.

commands.what: Searches file names by pattern; `-iname` ignores upper/lower case.
commands.where: When looking for files with a certain extension in a project.
commands.why: You scan the whole tree in seconds without browsing by hand.

commands.what: Filters by type: `f` file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link.
commands.where: When you only want directories or only files.
commands.why: Lets you set permissions for directories and files separately instead of a blanket `chmod -R`.

commands.what: Filters by size (`-size +1M`), modification day (`-mtime +7` = older than 7 days), permissions (`-perm 644`) or owner (`-user alice`).
commands.where: In clean-ups, security audits, hunting old logs.
commands.why: Finding the right file is cheaper than deleting the wrong one.

commands.what: Runs the command for EACH match separately; `{}` is replaced by the path. End it with `+` and the paths are collected and passed to a single call.
commands.where: When applying `chmod`, `ls -l`, `wc` and the like to every file.
commands.why: Bulk processing without a loop; the `+` form starts far fewer processes.

commands.what: Deletes matches directly; there is no undo.
commands.where: When cleaning up temporary files.
commands.why: Faster than `-exec rm` (one process). Put conditions BEFORE `-delete`, otherwise everything is deleted.

sections.tip: Habit: first `find ... -print`, read the output, then append `-delete` or `-exec`.
sections.danger: `find . -delete` with no condition deletes EVERYTHING in the current tree. Order matters: `-name` first, `-delete` last.

sections.title: xargs and command substitution
body: `rm`, `cp`, `wc` expect file names as **arguments** and do not read them from a pipe (stdin). `xargs` turns the lines on stdin into arguments for that command.

File names may contain spaces or newlines. The safe way: `find ... -print0 | xargs -0 ...`; names are separated by the NUL character. A plain `| xargs rm` hits the wrong file when names contain spaces.
`$(command)` inserts a command's output into the command line. It is an alternative to `xargs` but can hit the argument-length limit on very long lists.

commands.what: Runs a command and passes it the input from stdin as arguments.
commands.where: When feeding the output of `find` or `grep -l` into `rm`, `wc`, `chmod`.
commands.why: Fills the gap of the pipe: output becomes arguments.

commands.what: Separates names with NUL and hands them to xargs; safe with spaces and odd characters.
commands.where: For irreversible bulk jobs such as deleting and moving.
commands.why: A file called `my file.txt` is not split into two arguments.

commands.what: Command substitution: the inner command's output becomes part of the outer command.
commands.where: When adding a date to a file name or `hostname` to a message.
commands.why: You build commands with dynamic values.

sections.warn: `xargs` may run the command once even on empty input (GNU: prevent with `-r`). For dangerous commands first use `xargs echo rm` to see what would run.

sections.title: Streams, redirection and pipelines
body: Every process has three streams: 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr. `>` redirects stdout (1), `2>` redirects stderr. `2>&1` means "send stderr to wherever stdout currently goes"; **order matters**: `cmd > f 2>&1` writes both to the file, `cmd 2>&1 > f` leaves errors on screen.
Throw noise into `/dev/null`: `cmd 2> /dev/null`. In Bash, `&>` redirects both stdout and stderr; the portable form is `> f 2>&1`.
The classic log-summary pattern: `cut -d' ' -f2 run.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`. `uniq` only merges adjacent lines, which is why `sort` must come first.

commands.what: `2> f` writes errors to a file; `> f 2>&1` writes output and errors to the same file.
commands.where: When collecting script output in a log file.
commands.why: You record errors without losing them; the order is essential.

commands.what: Throws the output away.
commands.where: When you only care about the exit code, not the output.
commands.why: Keeps the screen clean: `grep -q` or `cmd 2> /dev/null`.

commands.what: Feeds several lines into the command's stdin; ends when `EOF` stands alone on a line.
commands.where: When creating scripts or configuration files.
commands.why: With a quoted `<<'EOF'` variables are not expanded; the text goes in literally.
commands.example:
cat > notes2.txt <<'EOF'
line one
line two
EOF

commands.what: Writes stdin to the screen and to a file; `-a` appends.
commands.where: When saving an intermediate result in the middle of a pipeline.
commands.why: You see and store at once. `| sudo tee f` solves the permission problem of `sudo cmd > f`.

commands.what: Counts lines and sorts them from most to least frequent.
commands.where: In log, IP and error-frequency analysis.
commands.why: One line answers "which occurs most"; add `| head -n 3` for the top three.

sections.tip: `wc -l` counts lines; `head -n 1` gives the first line, `tail -n 5` the last five. Combined they make quick log checks.

sections.title: Quoting, expansion and exit codes
body: The shell expands before running: `$VARIABLE`, `$(...)`, globs (`*.log`) and braces (`{a,b}`). Quotes control this expansion.
Double quotes `"..."` expand variables and `$(...)` but block globbing. Single quotes `'...'` expand nothing. Always protect values with spaces using double quotes.
Every command returns an exit code: 0 means success, anything else an error. `$?` shows the last one. `&&` continues only on success, `||` only on failure.

commands.what: Single quotes leave text unchanged; double quotes allow `$` expansion.
commands.where: When writing variables, names with spaces and patterns.
commands.why: `echo "$HOME"` prints the path, `echo '$HOME'` prints the text `$HOME`.

commands.what: The shell expands the pattern to file names; `*` is anything, `?` one character.
commands.where: When selecting several files with one command.
commands.why: Unquoted, the pattern arrives mangled at `find -name`; if `*.log` matches nothing it stays as typed.

commands.what: The shell turns `{a,b,c}` into three words; it does not look at files, it only generates text.
commands.where: When creating several files or directories.
commands.why: `mkdir -p project/{src,docs}` creates two directories with one command.

commands.what: `a && b`: b only if a succeeded. `a || b`: b only if a failed. `;` always continues.
commands.where: For tasks with a precondition: `cd dir && rm ...`.
commands.why: If `cd` fails, the following delete does not run in the wrong directory.

sections.warn: Write `cd logs && rm *.tmp` instead of `cd logs; rm *.tmp`: if `cd` fails, `;` still runs `rm` in the directory you are in.

sections.title: Your first script: shebang and running it
body: A script is a text file containing commands. The first line, the **shebang** (`#!/bin/bash`), names the interpreter. To run it the file needs the `x` permission.

`./script.sh` runs the file from the current directory. If you type just `script.sh`, the shell only searches the directories in `PATH`; the current directory is deliberately not in it (security). `bash script.sh` works even without `x`.
Script arguments are `$1`, `$2` …, the exit code is `$?`. In small scripts you can set a default with `name="${1:-world}"`.

commands.what: First line of the script; tells the kernel the interpreter.
commands.where: At the top of every executable script.
commands.why: It is clear which shell runs the script, keeping behaviour consistent across distributions.

commands.what: Adds the execute permission to the file.
commands.where: Before running your script directly.
commands.why: Without `x`, `./script.sh` says "Permission denied".

commands.what: Runs the script by path; arguments follow.
commands.where: For scripts in the current directory.
commands.why: No `PATH` lookup; exactly the file you chose runs.

commands.what: Shows the exit code of the last command (0 = success).
commands.where: When checking a command's success by hand or in a script.
commands.why: `&&`, `||` and `if` all use this code.

sections.tip: For your own scripts you can add `~/bin` to `PATH`: `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`. Make it permanent in `~/.bashrc`.

t01.text: In the `lab` directory list all `.tmp` files with `find`: `find . -name "*.tmp"`.
t01.hint: Put the pattern in double quotes.

t02.text: Count the `ERROR` lines in `run.log` and write the number to the file `count.txt`: `grep -c ERROR run.log > count.txt`.
t02.hint: `-c` gives the number of matching lines.

t03.text: Write `host: ` and the machine name into the file `who.txt`: `echo "host: $(hostname)" > who.txt`.

t04.text: Create the directory `backup`, then use a glob to copy all `.log` files from `logs` into it: `cp logs/*.log backup/`.
t04.hint: First `mkdir backup`; `cp` takes the target last.

t05.text: First write the error to `err.txt`: `ls missing.txt 2> err.txt`. Then write output AND error of `ls missing.txt notes.txt` together into `both.txt`.

t06.text: With `printf` write the script `greet.sh` (shebang + `echo "Hello $1"`), make it executable with `chmod +x greet.sh` and run `./greet.sh alice > greet.out`.
t06.hint: `printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "Hello $1"\n' > greet.sh`; use single quotes, otherwise `$1` is expanded immediately.

t07.text: PREDICT: Which level does `cut -d' ' -f2 run.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` show most often, and how many times? Guess first, then run it.
t07.hint: The second field is the level (`INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`). Count the lines.

t08.text: PREDICT: What does `echo "$HOME" '$HOME'` print? Guess, then run it.
t08.hint: Double quotes expand, single quotes do not.

t09.text: PREDICT: What does `grep -q FATAL run.log || echo none` print? Guess, then run it.
t09.hint: Without `FATAL`, `grep` returns 1; then `||` runs the right-hand command.

t10.text: DEBUG: Someone typed `find . -name *.log` and got only `run.log`; the files under `logs/` are missing. Fix the command and write the full list to `all_logs.txt`.
t10.hint: First run `find . -name *.log` and see: the shell expanded `*.log` to `run.log`. Quote the pattern.

t11.text: DEBUG: `./hello.sh` says "Permission denied". Fix it and run it; the result must end up in `hello.out`.
t11.hint: Check the permissions with `ls -l hello.sh`; then `chmod +x hello.sh`.

t12.text: MINI PROJECT: Filter the `ERROR` lines, show them and save them to `errors.txt` at once (`tee`), then append the output of `wc -l errors.txt` to `summary.txt` with `>>`.
t12.hint: `grep ERROR run.log | tee errors.txt`, then `wc -l errors.txt >> summary.txt`.

t13.text: CHALLENGE: Delete all `.tmp` files under `project` using `find` and `-exec rm {} \;`. (The simulator does not run `-exec`; the correct syntax is checked.)
t13.hint: `find project -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \;`; the `\;` matters. On a real VM test with `-print` first.

t14.text: CHALLENGE: Get the line count of all `.txt` files the safe way: `-print0` with `xargs -0` and `wc -l`. (`xargs` is not in the simulator; the syntax is checked.)

t15.text: CHALLENGE: In `access.log` find the most frequent IP with its count and write only that single line to `top.txt`.
t15.hint: `cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 1 > top.txt`.

t16.text: TICKET #3901 — Support: "For the morning meeting we need a script that writes the `ERROR` and `WARN` lines from `run.log` to `problems.txt`, sorted; we will run it daily." Write `check.sh` (shebang + `grep -E ... | sort > problems.txt`), make it executable and run it.
t16.hint: Write it with `printf` or `echo` in single quotes, `chmod +x check.sh`, `./check.sh`.

vm.intro: Do the following steps on your own VM (Ubuntu, Rocky or Alma). Try everything under `~/adv`; never use `-delete` or `rm -r` where real data lives.

v01.title: Set up a practice area and search with find
v01.text: Build a practice tree, then search with `find` by name, type and size. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/adv/logs ~/adv/project/src
touch ~/adv/logs/app.log ~/adv/logs/old.log ~/adv/project/a.tmp ~/adv/project/src/b.tmp
echo data > ~/adv/project/src/main.txt
find ~/adv -name "*.log"
find ~/adv -type d
find ~/adv -type f -size -1k

differs: The order of `find` output depends on the file system; what matters is that all `.log` files appear.
If your user is not `student`, the start of the path differs; that is fine.

v02.title: -exec, + and xargs
v02.text: Apply first `-exec ... \;`, then `-exec ... +` and `xargs -0` to the same files. Notice: `\;` starts one command per file, `+` batches.

blocks.expected:
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 0 Nov 12 10:00 /home/student/adv/project/a.tmp
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 0 Nov 12 10:00 /home/student/adv/project/src/b.tmp

differs: With `+` the `ls -l` output usually comes sorted by path, with `\;` in find order. The content is the same.
The message `find: missing argument to '-exec'` means the trailing `\;` or `+` is missing.

v03.title: List first, then delete
v03.text: First take a **snapshot** of your VM. `-delete` is irreversible: see what would be deleted, then delete only inside `~/adv`. Press "Done" afterwards.

blocks.cmd:
# Dry run first
find ~/adv -name "*.tmp" -print
# If correct, delete (condition BEFORE -delete)
find ~/adv -name "*.tmp" -delete
find ~/adv -name "*.tmp"

differs: If the last command still lists files, `-delete` may be missing or you are in the wrong directory; check with `pwd`.

v04.title: Log analysis: here-document and pipeline
v04.text: Write a sample log with a here-document, then count the levels and redirect the error stream.

blocks.cmd:
cat > ~/adv/run.log <<'EOF'
10:01 INFO start
10:02 ERROR disk full
10:03 WARN slow disk
10:04 INFO retry
10:05 ERROR timeout
10:06 INFO ok
EOF
cut -d' ' -f2 ~/adv/run.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
ls /nonexistent ~/adv/run.log > ~/adv/both.txt 2>&1
cat ~/adv/both.txt
blocks.expected:
3 INFO
      2 ERROR
      1 WARN
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory
/home/student/adv/run.log

differs: If numbers or spacing differ, check the log lines: the second field of each line must be the level.
On a localised system the error message is translated; you will see local text instead of `No such file`.

v05.title: Your first script
v05.text: Write the script, try to run it without `x`, grant the permission, run it again and look at the exit code.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/adv
cat > hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
name="${1:-world}"
echo "Hello, $name"
EOF
./hello.sh
chmod +x hello.sh
./hello.sh student
echo $?

differs: If the first `./hello.sh` works, your file system (e.g. some WSL mounts) already grants `x`.
If you see `hello.sh: command not found`, you forgot the `./` prefix; the current directory is not in `PATH`.

q1.q: What is the difference between `find ... -exec rm {} \;` and `find ... -exec rm {} +`?
options: `\;` applies only to directories, `+` only to files
`\;` runs the command once per file, `+` collects the paths and passes them to a few calls
`+` never runs the command, it only lists
There is no difference, only a style
q1.explain: `\;` starts one process per match; `+` collects arguments and gets by with far fewer processes.

options: The shell expands `*.log` to names in the current directory before `find` starts
The command deletes the whole disk
q2.explain: The shell does the expanding. Quote the pattern as `"*.log"` so it reaches `find` unchanged.

q3.q: Which command writes both output and errors to `out.txt`?
q3.explain: stdout is redirected to the file first, then stderr goes "where stdout now goes". In the reverse order the error stays on screen.

q4.q: How do you safely pass `find` results to `rm` when file names contain spaces?
q4.explain: `-print0` and `xargs -0` separate names with NUL; names containing spaces or newlines are not split.

summary: `find` walks trees; quote patterns, list first, then add `-delete`/`-exec`.
`-exec ... \;` per file, `-exec ... +` and `xargs` in batches; the safe pair: `-print0 | xargs -0`.
`>` stdout, `2>` stderr, `2>&1` merges (order matters), `/dev/null` is the bin, `tee` shows and saves.
`sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` finds the most frequent entries; combine with `head`/`tail`/`wc -l`.
Double quotes expand, single quotes do not; `&&` on success, `||` on failure.

glossary.meaning: File name patterns like `*`, `?`, `[...]` that the shell expands.
Standard output (1) and standard error (2) streams.
Passing multi-line text as a command's input with `<<EOF`.
`|` connects the output of one command to the input of the next.
The first script line `#!/bin/bash`; it names the interpreter.
Number a command returns when it ends; 0 success, otherwise error. Read with `$?`.
The `\0` byte that separates names; `-print0` and `xargs -0` use it.
